frozen_original.title: Supreme Court Grants Trump Broad Presidential Immunity — Delays All Federal Cases
frozen_original.synopsis: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court issued a landmark 6-3 ruling in Trump v. United States, granting former presidents broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts conducted while in office. The ruling — the first time the Supreme Court addressed presidential criminal immunity — dramatically narrowed the scope of Special Counsel Jack Smith's federal indictment against Trump related to the 2020 election interference scheme. The decision required lower courts to determine which of Trump's alleged acts were "official" and thus immune, effectively delaying the federal trial past the November 2024 election. Critics argued the ruling placed presidents above the law and created conditions for future authoritarian abuse of power.

frozen_original_record.synopsis: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court issued a landmark 6-3 ruling in Trump v. United States, granting former presidents broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office. The ruling, written by Chief Justice John Roberts with the conservative majority, effectively shielded Trump from prosecution for many of the acts alleged in Jack Smith's January 6 indictment. The decision remanded cases back to lower courts to determine what constituted 'official' versus 'unofficial' acts, causing massive delays. Legal scholars and the three liberal justices warned the ruling fundamentally altered the constitutional principle that no one is above the law and created a de facto monarchy.
frozen_original_record.title: Supreme Court Grants Trump Broad Presidential Immunity — Delays All Federal Cases

merged_description_snapshot.description_long:
On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court issued a 6–3 decision in Trump v. United States addressing whether a former president could face criminal prosecution for conduct during his time in office. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the conservative majority, which recognized broad immunity from prosecution for official presidential acts. The Court did not decide that every act alleged in the January 6 case was protected; it remanded the matter so lower courts could determine which alleged conduct was official and which was unofficial.

That classification required further proceedings and delayed consideration of Jack Smith’s federal indictment. The decision therefore affected the timing and legal path of the case against Donald Trump, while leaving unresolved how the immunity framework would apply to specific allegations. The supplied account describes the ruling as effectively shielding Trump from prosecution for many of the acts alleged, but the case-specific determinations were left to the lower courts.

The ruling also changed the legal framework for presidential criminal accountability. In dissent, the three liberal justices warned about its constitutional implications; Sonia Sotomayor was among them. Legal scholars likewise raised concerns that the decision weakened the principle that no one is above the law. Those warnings were critiques of the ruling’s potential consequences, not findings that the United States had become a monarchy. The central unresolved question was how broadly the official-act immunity would apply in future prosecutions and in the proceedings on remand.
merged_description_snapshot.description_medium: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in Trump v. United States that former presidents have broad criminal immunity for official acts in office. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion. The Court sent the case back to lower courts to distinguish official from unofficial conduct, a process that delayed proceedings related to Jack Smith’s January 6 indictment. The three liberal justices warned of serious constitutional consequences.

frozen_original.title: Trump Claims 'Absolute Immunity' for Any Presidential Action
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump and his legal team formally asserted in April 2025 that the Supreme Court's July 2024 immunity ruling in Trump v. United States granted him absolute immunity from accountability for essentially any action taken in office, including actions clearly outside core executive functions. The expansive interpretation went far beyond what even the conservative Supreme Court majority had written, claiming that virtually any presidential act could be characterized as official and thus immune from criminal or civil accountability. Constitutional scholars described the claim as incompatible with the rule of law and the principle that no person is above the law. The claim was being tested in multiple ongoing criminal and civil proceedings against Trump.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Investigate Judge Juan Merchan Who Presided Over Hush Money Trial
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 25, 2025, days after returning to office, Trump publicly threatened to direct investigations against Judge Juan Merchan — the New York state judge who had presided over Trump's hush money criminal trial and had sentenced him — calling him a 'crooked judge' and suggesting Merchan and his family should face scrutiny. While Merchan was a state judge and largely beyond federal executive reach, the public threat from a sitting president against a judge who had ruled against him sent a clear message of retaliatory intent to the entire judiciary. Legal scholars noted the threat was part of a coordinated intimidation campaign against the legal system as a whole, targeting judges at every level. New York court officials condemned the threats and took additional security precautions for Merchan and his family. The episode was widely cited as evidence of Trump's intent to use the presidency to pursue personal vendettas against the legal system.

merged_description_snapshot.description_long: Trump Media & Technology Group announced a paid, licensed Truth API feed intended to give banks and trading firms faster access to posts from the ten most influential Truth Social accounts. Reuters reported that, before the launch, the company had discussed charging up to $100,000 per month, or $60,000 monthly for a three-year commitment. Reuters also reported that the company said customers had signed up ahead of launch, but did not identify them; the reported offer prices came from unnamed sources. The product raises questions about whether financial firms can receive Trump’s posts before ordinary users and news outlets, particularly when posts announce tariffs or other government actions. A press-freedom group and a media outlet later sued, arguing that the feed sold government information; Trump Media responded that the posts were widely available. The sources establish a commercial data product and reported pricing, but they do not provide an official determination that each post is a presidential record or establish that the service violated records law. The legal status of the posts and the boundaries between the company’s feed and government records remain unresolved.
